terms.gloss: know (a person, a place, something one is familiar with)
terms.grammar: verb: perfect of nōscō with present sense (nōstī, nōram, nōsse)
terms.comment: Properly “I have got to know”, so “I know”; nōveram or nōram is “I knew”. Latin keeps sciō for facts and nōvī for acquaintance: ut vīlicus nātūram agrī nōvit, dispēnsātor litterās scit (Cic. Rep. 5.3.5, cited by Lewis & Short, s.v. sciō).

terms.gloss: get to know, learn; in the perfect, know
terms.comment: Lewis & Short: in the perfect tenses “to know”, very frequent in every period.

terms.gloss: get to know (in the present tenses)
terms.comment: The present means “get to know”: told “I don’t know him”, a character in Plautus answers at nōsce sānē, “well, get to know him, then” (Plaut. As. 464).

phrases.latin: nam mellītus erat suamque nōrat ipsam tam bene quam puella mātrem
phrases.english: for he was sweet as honey, and knew his mistress as well as a little girl knows her mother

phrases.latin: ego, ille quem nōstī, aprōs trēs et quidem pulcherrimōs cēpī
phrases.english: I, yes, the man you know, have caught three boars, and fine ones too

phrases.latin: Ulixēs, quem nōstī, vir ille cui Aeolus ventōs in utre clausōs dedit
phrases.english: Ulysses, whom you know, the man Aeolus gave the winds to, shut up in a bag
